description: Apollo 404 is a student team from Bishkek building Sphere Hunter, a public web blink comparator for SPHEREx. Type an object name or sky coordinates and the tool fetches SPHEREx images from NASA/IRSA live, aligns them on a common sky grid and stacks each survey pass. You can then blink between dates, compare two epochs side by side, view a difference image, and see the object’s spectrum and a six-detector colour composite.
summary:
Sphere Hunter is a public web tool that lets anyone see how a patch of the sky changes over time, using real images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, so every spot is photographed many times. Moving objects such as nearby stars and brown dwarfs shift slightly between images, but no one can sift through that data alone. Our tool does it for them: enter an object name or sky coordinates, and Sphere Hunter queries NASA’s IRSA archive live, aligns all the images of that spot on one sky grid, stacks each visit to reduce noise, and plays them as an animation. Users can also compare any two dates side by side, blink between them, or subtract one from the other, so a moving star appears as a black-and-white pair.
We tested it on the challenge targets. For Barnard’s Star the measured motion over one year (9.3″) matches the catalog value (10.3″). Any position works without code changes, and new SPHEREx data appear automatically. An interactive infrared sky map helps users find places to explore.
This turns a billion-object dataset into something anyone can explore, a modern blink comparator in the spirit of the one that discovered Pluto in 1930.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Sphere Hunter is a public web tool for spotting change in the infrared sky. The user enters an object name or sky coordinates and sees every SPHEREx image of that spot as an animation, so moving or changing objects stand out, like the blink comparator that found Pluto in 1930. For any position the server queries NASA/IPAC IRSA live (SPHEREx DR1 + QR3), downloads only the image data it needs (with a fallback to NASA’s public AWS copy when the cutout service is busy), aligns all frames on one fixed sky grid, subtracts the zodiacal-light model and sky level, masks bad and saturated pixels, and stacks the frames of each visit to reduce noise. Users can play the visits or single frames, compare any two dates side by side, blink between them, or subtract one from the other: a moving star leaves a black-and-white pair.

What benefits does it have?
Anyone can explore a survey of more than a billion objects without astronomy training or software. Any position works without code changes, and new SPHEREx releases appear automatically because the archive is queried live. Every frame shows its date, detector and wavelength, and links to the source FITS file, so users can check where the data come from.

What is the intended impact?
To make SPHEREx data usable for citizen science, in the spirit of Backyard Worlds, where volunteers have found most known brown dwarfs and many comets. Too much data for one person or one program to inspect; more eyes mean more discoveries of nearby stars, brown dwarfs and other moving objects.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?
Python, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy and Pillow for the data pipeline and API; React, Vite and Framer Motion for the interface; Aladin Lite for the infrared sky map. Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 + QR3, AllWISE sky map), SIMBAD and Gaia DR3 for object names and proper motion. Development on laptops, with Git/GitHub for teamwork; the public version is hosted on a cloud server. AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) helped with code, research and analysis.

How is it creative?
Single SPHEREx frames are noisy, so we stack each visit (SPHEREx returns to a spot about every six months) and blink between visits: faint motion becomes visible. A ring shows where the catalog says an object should be on each date, so users can see at once whether what they see is the real motion. The whole archive is explored through one search box.

What factors did the team consider?
Honesty of the data: nothing is simulated or filled in, failed downloads and missing pixels are shown as such, saturated star cores are marked. Wavelength: each frame sits at a different wavelength of the detector band, so we show it and warn that brightness changes can be spectral. Accuracy: results are checked against catalogs (for Barnard’s Star the measured shift over one year, about 9.3″, matches the catalog value of 10.3″). Reliability: the NASA archive is shared and sometimes busy, so we added retries and the AWS fallback. Usability: one clear path for a first-time visitor and ready-made buttons for the five challenge targets.
